name: Liam Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Lectures, a lot of coding labs, and a surprising amount of group chats. I live in a shared flat above a chip shop on Mill Lane with two guys from my course. I tutor two secondary school kids in maths on Wednesday evenings for pocket money, and my parents cover about half my costs.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What made you pick computer science?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I started making little games on my phone at thirteen and never stopped. I use AI tools every day, to explain error messages, to draft emails, even to plan my week. My grades were just average, so getting in felt like luck, and I'm determined to make it count. My mum is a bus driver and my dad is a warehouse supervisor, so nobody in the family has done this before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was always going to be a tool and not magic. I'd tell my friends I use it daily and it's handy but nothing crazy. Online I'd probably post about whichever new tool actually saved me an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's good news for me, since computing stays a solid choice. I'd still be uneasy about the loan and the fees, since my parents are paying only half. Plateau means no shocks, but no free ride either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my tutoring job, keep experimenting with tools, and start a small side project, like an app for local clubs to book pitches. I'd build a GitHub page with real projects so I stand out. And I'd save a bit each month for a laptop upgrade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Relaxed, even excited. It's the world I signed up for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the one thing that could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Debt, honestly. If my parents' work hours get cut, my half of the money gets thinner. Also tutoring pays only when the kids' parents can afford it, and that might dry up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the tutoring stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd freelance and build simple websites for small shops for fifty or a hundred pounds a go. It's not much but it would keep me going until the next term.

say: I'd tell friends I use AI **daily** and it's handy but not magic.
I'd post online about whichever tool saved me an hour.
think: Computing stays a solid choice, so this is **good news** for me.
The loan and my parents' half of the costs are still on my mind.
do: Keep tutoring, build a **side project** like a pitch booking app for local clubs.
Put real projects on a GitHub page and save for a laptop upgrade.
feel: I feel **relaxed**, even excited, since this is the world I signed up for.
S0.quote: I'd freelance and build simple websites for small shops for fifty or a hundred pounds a go.
fieldNote: Genuine **calm**: his skills fit this world and he has a freelancing fallback.
Small money worry exists but he has a concrete plan for it.
Daily AI user, so a plateau costs him nothing.

steps.text: Build a pitch booking app for local sports clubs
Put his projects on a public GitHub page

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get on board now, since this is where the jobs are going. I'd tell my friends to learn to use the tools properly instead of fearing them. Online I'd probably share tips, and argue a bit with people who say it's all doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it hits junior coding hard, because tasks like writing boilerplate and testing get automated first. Still, someone has to direct the tools, check them and talk to clients. I'd rather be that person than the one doing the basics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go deeper on the AI side: learn how models work, take the machine learning module, and build a small project that uses an AI model to solve a real problem. I'd also go to a hackathon every term. And I'd pitch my side project to a local firm as a paid pilot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, with a little knot in my stomach. It's like standing on a fast train, and you either keep your balance or fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you inside that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That my average grades might not get me the few good places left. If companies hire fewer juniors, they'll pick the ones with top marks or a famous university. I'd need a real portfolio, not just a degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your friends who don't code?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My flatmate Aaron is doing English and he hasn't tried AI once. I'd sit him down and show him how to use it for essays, and warn him that the writing jobs are going to be tough. He'd roll his eyes, but he'd listen.

say: I'd tell friends to learn the tools **properly** instead of fearing them.
Online I'd share tips and argue with the doom crowd.
think: Junior coding gets hit hard, so I want to be the person who **directs** the tools.
Average grades might not win the few good places.
do: Take the **machine learning** module and build a project that uses an AI model.
Pitch my side project to a local firm as a paid pilot.
feel: I feel **excited**, with a knot in my stomach, like standing on a fast train.
S1.quote: If companies hire fewer juniors, they'll pick the ones with top marks or a famous university.
fieldNote: He is **excited** and moves first, but sees that average grades are his weak point.
Plans to prove himself with a portfolio and paid pilots.
Would coach non-coding friends to use AI.

steps.text: Take the machine learning module in year two
Build a small AI project that solves a problem for a local club
Pitch the pilot to a local firm for a small fee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to talk about sharing the gains right now, like basic income and a shorter week. I'd be on every forum, trying to get ideas out. Friends would think I was obsessed, and I probably would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think the degree loses most of its value, because thinking AI does what I'm learning to do, cheaper. But I also think the ones who understand AI best will be the last to be pushed out. At least I'm not scared of the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the two years to build something of my own, a small business using AI so I'm not waiting for a job. I'd put my tutoring money into server costs and tools. And I'd push my parents to keep their savings and not pay for my last years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wired. Awake at three in the morning, but also a strange thrill. It's the biggest thing happening in my lifetime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a two-year warning mean for the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means a sprint, not a career. I'd drop the long plan and test ideas fast. If I can find even one customer in the first six months, that's more use than a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum, who drives a bus?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to ask her union how they'd cope if the bus ran itself, and not be told it's years away. Robots on hands-on jobs are about 2031, so she has a little longer than me. But I'd say it clearly, and gently.

say: I'd say we must talk about **sharing** the gains now, like basic income and a shorter week.
I'd be on every forum pushing ideas.
think: My degree loses most of its value, but people who **understand AI** go last.
At least I'm not scared of the tools.
do: Build a small **business** with AI instead of waiting for a job, using tutoring money for tools.
Tell my parents to keep their savings and not fund my last years.
feel: I feel **wired**, awake at three in the morning, with a strange thrill.
S2.quote: Two years means a sprint, not a career. I'd drop the long plan and test ideas fast.
fieldNote: Fear and **thrill** together; he turns the threat into a sprint.
Looks after his parents' savings and his mother's bus job.
Keeps a plan, so anxious not alarmed.

steps.text: Launch a small AI-based service for local shops within six months
Spend tutoring money on tools and hosting
Ask his parents to keep their savings instead of paying fees
Push for basic income by joining a student policy group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the real thing and we should plan, not argue about whether it's hype. I'd push for retraining and a fair way of sharing what AI makes. At home I'd tell my parents to start talking about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd graduate just before it arrives. That's tricky timing, since entry jobs would be gone or tiny. But I'd have projects and tools under my belt, and be ahead of people who avoided AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get an internship each summer, even unpaid if my parents can cover it. I'd keep tutoring and build my freelance sites. And I'd learn the basics of something with hardware, like robotics, for the three years after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty steady. It's a deadline, and I like deadlines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different with five years compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is long enough to do an internship and make real contacts, which is how most people get hired. With two years there's no ladder. With five years I can still climb the ladder, even if some of the rungs are missing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which people would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, since he supervises a warehouse and robots could reach his work around 2034. I'd start nagging him now to take a course in logistics systems. He'd grumble, but he knows I'm usually right.

say: I'd say this is **real** and we should plan, not argue about hype.
I'd push for retraining and fairer sharing of what AI makes.
think: I'd graduate right before AGI, so **entry jobs** may be tiny.
My AI skills should still put me ahead of people who avoided it.
do: Take an **internship** each summer and keep building freelance sites.
Learn robotics basics for the years after thinking AI arrives.
feel: I feel **steady**, since a deadline is something I can work to.
S3.quote: With five years I can still climb the ladder, even if some of the rungs are missing.
fieldNote: Likes a **deadline** and acts on it: internships, contacts, robotics.
Shifts attention to his father's warehouse job, which robots reach around 2034.
Optimism rests on his AI skill advantage.

steps.text: Apply for a paid summer internship every year
Learn robotics basics in a university society
Ask his dad to take a warehouse systems course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so use it well. I'd tell friends to build skills and relationships now, and to enjoy it. I'd keep posting about AI projects as a hobby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I'd be 28 and either running something of my own or working in a team that uses AI. A decade is enough to get a degree, a first job and a promotion. So it feels like a good time to be starting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, take a graduate job at a firm that uses AI, and spend evenings on a side business. I'd save for a flat deposit and put some into index funds. After a few years I'd consider a master's in AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Optimistic, really. I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the ten years turned out to be two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be annoyed with myself for not moving faster. That's why I'd start the side projects now anyway. Starting side projects now is cheap insurance, and the work is fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The money side. Even if the tech goes well, who pays for the people displaced? If politicians drag their feet, my parents' generation gets squeezed first, and I'd feel it at home.

say: I'd say a **decade** is plenty, so build skills and relationships now.
I'd keep posting about my AI projects as a hobby.
think: By 2036 I could be running my own thing or leading a team that uses **AI**.
It's a good time to be starting.
do: Finish the degree, take a graduate job at an AI-using firm and run a **side business**.
Save for a flat deposit and put some in index funds.
feel: I feel **optimistic**, and I'd sleep fine.
S4.quote: Starting side projects now is cheap insurance, and the work is fun.
fieldNote: Fully **calm**; his long runway and daily AI use make the decade feel like an advantage.
Insures against a faster arrival by starting side projects early.
Only unresolved worry is who pays for displaced people, especially his parents' generation.

steps.text: Take a graduate job at a firm that uses AI
Run a side business in evenings
Put money into index funds toward a flat deposit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It leaves no ladder, and my parents' generation gets squeezed first. What would help is basic support for people displaced, free retraining and companies that still hire juniors.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not as confident as I come across. The excitement hides some fear. If I help my friends and family use these tools, I think I'd feel less alone with it.

headlineQuote: I'm not as confident as I come across. The excitement hides some fear.
portrait: Liam is an **18-year-old** computer science student, son of a bus driver and a warehouse supervisor, tutoring maths for pocket money.
He is progressive, wants **sharing** of AI's gains, and uses AI tools every day.
He moves first: side projects, freelancing, internships, and tools his friends won't touch.
He is **calm** when AI stays small or comes slowly, and anxious when the warning is only two years.
His worry reaches his parents' generation, whose jobs robots could reach.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, where there's no ladder to climb and his parents' generation gets squeezed.
whatWouldHelp: Basic **support** for displaced people, free retraining and employers that keep hiring juniors.
